115.title: Comparison to AGP pseudoLocalesEnabled
115.content: AGP can build pseudolocalised values-en-rXA/strings.xml resources into the consumer’s APK at compile time, then load them at runtime via the standard locale qualifier path. This data product takes the opposite tack: leave strings.xml alone, intercept the lookup. The trade-offs: . |   | This product | AGP pseudoLocalesEnabled | . | Consumer config | none | buildTypes.<type>.pseudoLocalesEnabled = true | . | APK size | unchanged (renderer-only) | grows with pseudo resources | . | Runtime cost | Resources.getText wrap, ~free | none (resources resolved by framework) | . | Off-by-default | yes — only triggers when localeTag in {en-XA, ar-XB} | yes — opt-in per build type | . | Works in production app | no — preview / render only | yes | . For preview rendering specifically — which is what this tool is for — the runtime path is strictly cheaper and simpler. Production apps that ship pseudolocalised resources for QA still want AGP.

121.title: Payload shape
121.content: RecompositionPayload, RecompositionNode in :data-recomposition-core. // compose/recomposition (schemaVersion 2) { "mode": "delta", // or "snapshot" "sinceFrameStreamId": "f-7a1c", // populated in delta mode "inputSeq": 2, // monotonic per flushed delta "nodes": [ // reason: PARAMETER_CHANGE | STATE_READ | BOTH | UNKNOWN { "nodeId": "1a2b3c4d", "count": 1, "reason": "STATE_READ" }, { "nodeId": "5e6f7a8b", "count": 1, "reason": "PARAMETER_CHANGE" } ] } . Each node’s reason is attributed from the Compose runtime’s onScopeInvalidated(scope, value) signal compared against the recompose count: a scope invalidated by a snapshot write it subscribed to reads STATE_READ, one that re-ran only because its caller did reads PARAMETER_CHANGE, and a mix reads BOTH. This is the “why did this recompose?” signal — a parent reading state and forwarding it as parameters shows up as one STATE_READ dragging a fan of PARAMETER_CHANGE children. Nodes also carry nullable bounds ({x, y, width, height}) and source-marker fields (sourceFile / sourceLine / sourceColumn / functionName) for the heat-map and source-overlay surfaces. These are present on the v2 wire but not yet populated — the post-layout bounds join and slot-table reflection that fill them are deferred increments (see issue #1605).

147.title: How a LONG capture is verified
147.content: Every stride of the walk and every seam of the stitch is checked against the pixels, and what could not be checked is written next to the PNG. The driver measures each stride. ScrollBy on a lazy list animates, and a lazy list’s ScrollAxisRange.value is not a pixel position (LazyColumn and Wear’s ScalingLazyColumn publish index × 500 + offset), so neither “has the spring landed” nor “how far did the content move” can be read off the semantics range. driveScrollByViewport instead snapshots the on-screen positions of the scrollable’s descendant semantics nodes before each stride, advances the paused clock frame by frame until they stop moving, measures the median displacement of the nodes seen on both sides, and dispatches a corrective ScrollBy (up to three) when the landing misses the planned stride by more than a pixel while the scroller still has room. The measured travel is the offset the stitcher receives, flagged as measured so the search window around it is a few pixels rather than a third-to-triple of the hint. The stitcher only aligns on signal. Rows are weighted by their horizontal luminance stddev, so black background and the body of a button between its text lines contribute nothing and a row through text or an icon decides the match. A candidate shift is only eligible when its overlap is at least a tenth of the viewport and its informative rows sum to enough signal to be a feature rather than a stray edge; candidates within a small margin of the best score are a tie and the one nearest the hint wins (identical chip bodies one pitch apart). This is what a pinned Wear TimeText used to defeat: with the time drawn over the head of every slice, a 12-row all-black overlap at the far end of the window out-scored the true shift and the next slice was painted from its top row, 10:10 and all. Chrome that appears at the foot of a slice is set aside. The last stride of a Wear walk lands at the content end, and landing there reveals the ScreenScaffold’s EdgeButton: the last slice’s bottom fifth is a bright button where the previous slice had background. At the true shift every row above it agrees exactly and every row of it disagrees violently, which misalignment never looks like (it spreads disagreement across the overlap). A candidate’s score therefore walks up from the bottom of the overlap past a contiguous run of disagreeing rows, caps it at a third of the overlap, and scores only the rows above; the run is reported as revealedRows on the seam. RevealedBottomChromeSeamTest pins this on the real slice pair. What is reported. Each seam gets a verdict — verified, low_signal (too little varied content in the overlap to decide on) or mismatch (no shift made the two slices agree) — and each stride a landed/not-landed outcome. The stitch is always written, but anything unverified rides in <png>.warnings.json: . { "unlandedScrollSteps": [{ "role": "…", "step": 2, "requestedPx": 307.2, "measuredPx": 225.0, "corrections": 0, "settled": true, "message": "…" }], "unverifiedScrollSeams": [{ "role": "…", "seam": 1, "verdict": "low_signal", "hintPx": 307, "shiftPx": 372, "overlapRows": 12, "informativeRows": 0, "residualPerPixel": 0.3, "message": "…" }] } . A clean capture writes neither array. A consumer that wants to refuse an untrustworthy tall PNG fails on either being non-empty; the renderer’s WearPinnedTimeTextLongScrollTest and LongScrollPreviewPixelTest do exactly that. To iterate on the matcher without a Robolectric round-trip, render with COMPOSEAI_KEEP_SCROLL_SLICES=1 (the per-slice PNGs, the settled final frame and the reported offsets stay in <id>_slices/ next to the output), then point COMPOSEAI_STITCH_HARNESS_DIR at that directory and run :data-scroll-core:test — ScrollSliceStitcherHarnessTest re-stitches every slice set it finds and prints each seam’s verdict.

174.title: UIAutomator hierarchy
174.content: A selector-shaped projection of Compose semantics: just enough metadata per node to formulate a UIAutomator-style By.text(...) / By.contentDescription(...) selector that uniquely targets it.

175.title: At a glance
175.content: |   |   | . | Kind | uia/hierarchy | . | Schema version | 2 | . | Modules | :data-uiautomator-core (published) · :data-uiautomator-hierarchy-android (published) · :data-uiautomator-connector | . | Render mode | default | . | Cost | low | . | Token usage | Inline JSON, not yet benchmarked (scales with selector node count). See token usage. | . | Transport | inline | . | Platforms | Android | .

176.title: What it answers
176.content: . | For each actionable node, what selector inputs are available — text, contentDescription, testTag, role? | Which uia.* actions does it support — uia.click, uia.scrollForward, uia.inputText, …? | What are the node’s root-relative bounds in source-bitmap pixels (boundsInRoot)? | Does the node have testTag ancestors that a hasParent({testTag: …}) / hasAncestor selector chain could resolve? | . The default filter keeps only nodes that expose at least one of the supported actions, dropping ~80% of layout-wrapper / pure-text nodes while still emitting everything an agent’s click / scroll / type could plausibly target. Snapshots can be taken against the merged semantics tree (the on-device UIAutomator default — Button { Text("Submit") } collapses into one node) or the unmerged tree.

177.title: What it does NOT answer
177.content: . | It is not a full SemanticsNode dump — for that, use compose/semantics. | It does not execute a selector — it gives you what is targetable; running a uia.click is the daemon’s renderNow path, not a data product fetch. | It does not include modifier or constraint detail; pair with layout/inspector when you need positioning context. | .

178.title: Use cases
178.content: . | Generate a UIAutomator-like end-to-end test plan for a screen without touching an emulator. | Confirm every actionable node has at least one stable selector input — fail review if a button has neither text, contentDescription, nor testTag. | Train an agent’s “which selector should I use” heuristic on the same shape it will see at runtime. | .

179.title: Payload shape
179.content: UiAutomatorHierarchyNode, Selector in :data-uiautomator-core. // uia/hierarchy { "nodes": [ { "text": "Submit", "contentDescription": null, "testTag": "submit-button", "testTagAncestors": ["checkout-screen"], "role": "Button", "actions": ["click"], "boundsInRoot": "48,200,144,232", "boundsInScreen": "48,200,144,232", "merged": true } ] } . boundsInScreen is a deprecated schema-v1 compatibility alias. Its value was always root-relative despite the name; schema v2 adds the accurately named boundsInRoot field.

180.title: Enabling
180.content: Producer runs once the UIAutomator extension is publicly enabled. Hierarchy snapshot is emitted by UiAutomatorHierarchyExtractor in :data-uiautomator-hierarchy-android (Android-only).

181.title: Companion products
181.content: . | Layout inspector — compose/semantics for the full SemanticsNode shape and layout/inspector for positioning. | Focus — compose/focus for the focused-node subset that a directional traversal would target. | Accessibility — a11y/hierarchy for the assistive-technology view of the same tree. | .

182.title: Wallpaper
182.content: Material You seed colour → derived ColorScheme, computed by the same algorithm Android uses for system wallpaper-driven theming (material-kolor / dynamic-color-utilities).

183.title: At a glance
183.content: |   |   | . | Kind | compose/wallpaper | . | Schema version | 1 | . | Modules | :data-wallpaper-core (published) · :data-wallpaper-connector | . | Render mode | default | . | Cost | low | . | Token usage | Inline JSON, not yet benchmarked. See token usage. | . | Transport | inline | . | Platforms | Android · Wear | .

184.title: What it answers
184.content: . | Given a seed colour and palette style, what Material 3 ColorScheme does the system derive? | How does the scheme change across TonalSpot, Vibrant, Expressive, Monochrome, etc.? | What does the same composable look like for three different wallpaper seeds without booting an emulator? | . The connector primes a WallpaperOverride so consumer code that reads the dynamic colour scheme sees the requested seed and palette style.

185.title: What it does NOT answer
185.content: . | It does not extract a seed from a real wallpaper bitmap — you supply the seed; that is upstream of this product. | It does not opine on contrast accessibility — pair with a11y/atf under the chosen scheme. | The schema of derivedColorScheme matches compose/theme’s colorScheme; for which composables consumed which token, fetch compose/theme instead. | .

186.title: Use cases
186.content: . | Render Material You previews of a “what does this app look like for users with different wallpapers” PR review. | Catch seeds that produce inaccessible contrast pairings on a critical CTA before they ship. | Build a marketing screenshot set across the standard Material You palette styles. | .

188.title: Enabling
188.content: Pass a WallpaperOverride on renderNow.overrides.wallpaper (MCP) to drive the seed / style / contrast / dark mode.

189.title: Companion products
189.content: . | Theme — compose/theme for the full Material 3 token set after the wallpaper-derived scheme is plugged in. | Ambient — compose/ambient for the Wear ambient-state side of the same render. | .

190.title: Wear OS in the simulator
190.content: A Wear OS APK is detected from its manifest (a required android.hardware.type.watch feature) and runs on a round 454×454 watch display. Configuration.isScreenRound() and the watch UI mode read as they do on a watch, rotary sends the crown’s scroll events, and screenshots are cropped to the circle. --launcher adds a Wear system UI around the app: a watch face, the app launcher, the notification stream, the tiles and widgets carousel, and quick settings. compose-preview android-simulator wear.apk --launcher # the app, over a watch face compose-preview android-simulator wear.apk --tile .MyTileService # a tile in the carousel compose-preview android-simulator --watchface face.apk # a WFF watch face, nothing else compose-preview android-simulator --watchface face.apk --install comp.apk # face + complication app compose-preview android-simulator phone.apk --pair wear.apk # a phone and its watch compose-preview android-simulator wear.apk --data-layer agent --control stdio # the agent as the phone . | On a watch | Goes to | Command | . | Back from the app’s root, or Home | the watch face | home | . | The side button | the launcher | key STEM_PRIMARY, launcher | . | Swipe up on the face | the notification stream | notifications {"op":"open"} | . | Swipe left or right on the face | the tiles and widgets carousel | tiles {"op":"next"} | . | Swipe down on the face | quick settings | quickSettings | .

191.title: Tiles and Wear Widgets
191.content: The carousel holds what you add, with --tile <service> (repeatable), tiles {"op":"add"}, or its own add page. | Tiles are bound by BIND_TILE_PROVIDER and called over their real AIDL: tile and resource requests, and the add / enter / leave / remove callbacks. They’re drawn by the protolayout tile renderer, which the CLI provides (apps don’t ship it). A LoadAction requests the tile again with the clicked state, and a LaunchAction starts its activity. | Wear Widgets (Glance Wear) are bound by BIND_WIDGET_PROVIDER, asked for a Remote Compose document at their container’s size, and played with the Remote Compose player. They’re shown the way a watch shows them: just the provider’s preferred container — small (2×1) or large (2×2), a stadium on a round watch and a squircle on a square one — with no card or label. | . Both read the watch’s simulated system data. health sets heart rate, steps, distance, calories and floors, which tiles read through PlatformHealthSources and widgets through Glance Wear’s HealthData. → {"cmd":"tiles","op":"add","component":".GoalsTileService"} → {"cmd":"health","heartRate":72,"steps":5400,"stepGoal":8000} → {"cmd":"screenshot","path":"tile.png"} .

192.title: Watch faces
192.content: --watchface <apk | package | component> (or watchface {"op":"set"}) replaces the demo face with one of two kinds: . | AndroidX watch faces (WatchFaceService, ListenableWatchFaceService) are bound through the library’s WatchFaceControlService and drawn headless, interactive or ambient. This is the same path Wear’s face editor and Android Studio’s previews use. | Declarative Watch Faces in the Watch Face Format (WFF, watch_face_info.xml) run one of two ways: . | Google’s runtime. When DeclarativeWatchFaceRuntime.apk is cached, the simulator hosts the WFF package in Google’s own runtime. The APK is never redistributed: compose-preview android-simulator dwf-runtime pull --from-adb copies it from your own Wear emulator, and dwf-runtime install <apk> registers a local copy. | The built-in compiler. Without the runtime (or with --dwf-runtime none), the face’s XML is compiled to Remote Compose and played in-process. | . Either way, [STEP_PERCENT], [BATTERY_PERCENT], [HEART_RATE], [WEATHER.*], [ACCELEROMETER_ANGLE_*], [CONFIGURATION.*] and [COMPLICATION.*] follow the simulated watch state. | . The clock, health, battery, weather and accel commands set that state, and ambient, tilt and palm move the screen between interactive, ambient and off. watchface {"op":"config"} sets user styles and ColorConfiguration options. Flavors switch too. Watch Face Push. An app calling WatchFacePushManager’s addWatchFace, updateWatchFace, listWatchFaces, removeWatchFace or setWatchFaceAsActive gets a simulated Watch Face Push service. The agent can push faces too, with watchface {"op":"push"}. Pushed WFF APKs are installed and activated live. Dynamic theme colors. By default (--theme-from-watchface), the active face’s accent palette becomes the system’s Material 3 dynamic colors, so Wear apps, tiles and Glance widgets that use dynamicColorScheme(context) follow the face. .

193.title: Complications
193.content: watchface {"op":"complication"} fills a slot from a ComplicationDataSourceService in one of these places: . | in the same APK as the face; | in another APK installed beside it with --install <comp.apk>. The ComplicationData crosses between the two simulator JVMs as real parcels. | . Without a component, the command fills the slot with an inline fake complication (type, text, title, value, min, max), so you can test a face’s slots without writing a data source. Timelines resolve against the simulated clock, and watchface {"op":"tap"} fires a complication’s tapAction. → {"cmd":"watchface","op":"complication","slot":0,"component":"com.example.comp/.StepsDataSource"} → {"cmd":"watchface","op":"complication","slot":1,"type":"RANGED_VALUE","value":62,"min":0,"max":100,"text":"62%"} → {"cmd":"watchface","op":"tap","slot":0} . For repeatable watch face checks, --scenario replays clock, health, battery, weather, ambient and tap steps headlessly. It asserts on the frame (changedFrom, litPixelRatio, regionColor) and on the watch face’s status, then writes report.json and exits 2 on failure.

194.title: Notifications, ongoing activities and ambient
194.content: . | The notification stream. Notifications are drawn the way Wear draws them from their extras: title, text, MessagingStyle, big picture, and WearableExtender actions and reply choices. A high-importance post peeks over the face. | Ongoing activities (androidx.wear.ongoing) appear as the face’s chip and as the launcher’s first rows, with their timers on the simulated clock. | Ambient mode. AmbientLifecycleObserver, the legacy AmbientModeSupport, Horologist’s AmbientAware and Wear Compose’s rememberAmbientModeManager() all get onEnterAmbient, onUpdateAmbient and onExitAmbient. An app that doesn’t support ambient is stopped and restarted as it would be on a watch. | .

195.title: Data Layer pairing
195.content: --pair <watch.apk> runs the watch app in a second simulator and connects the two apps with a simulated Wearable Data Layer. DataClient, MessageClient, NodeClient, CapabilityClient and ChannelClient answer from the simulator instead of Play services. Messages, requests, data items, assets, capabilities and channel streams cross between the apps and reach their live listeners and manifest WearableListenerServices. Each side is also a CompanionDeviceManager association. These work across the pair too: . | RemoteActivityHelper, including its availability status; | Horologist’s DataLayerAppHelper; | on the watch: RemoteAuthClient, BridgingManager and PhoneTypeHelper. | . With --control stdio, "device":"watch" sends a command to the watch, every line says which device it came from, and each crossing is a datalayer event. The agent as the peer. --data-layer agent needs no second app: the control channel plays the other device. Everything the app sends arrives as a datalayer send event, decoded as text or a DataMap when it can be. The agent answers with dataLayer actions: connect, disconnect, capabilities, put / delete, message / request, reply, and the channel operations. You can test a watch app’s sync, error and disconnected-phone paths without building the phone app. → {"cmd":"dataLayer","action":"connect","capabilities":["verify_remote_app"]} ← {"event":"datalayer","kind":"send","type":"message","path":"/start","requestId":4,"text":"…"} → {"cmd":"dataLayer","action":"reply","requestId":4,"text":"ok"} → {"cmd":"dataLayer","action":"put","path":"/settings","dataMap":{"units":"metric"}} .

196.title: Wear gaps
196.content: | Area | Gap | . | Watch faces | AndroidX GlesRenderer faces don’t run (Robolectric has no EGL); CanvasRenderer faces do. The on-watch face editor UI isn’t drawn: watchface {"op":"config"} sets options directly. | . | Declarative faces | Running Google’s own runtime needs your copy of DeclarativeWatchFaceRuntime.apk, pulled from a Wear emulator. The built-in compiler approximates the runtime, so it isn’t pixel-identical. scripts/dwf-diff.py renders a face both ways side by side when that matters. | . | Tiles | A tile’s TileUpdateRequester isn’t wired to the carousel: tiles {"op":"refresh"} requests it again. | . | Ambient | Ambient reaches the app, but nothing enforces it. The system doesn’t dim, shift for burn-in or cap the frame rate. Ambient offload and auto-resume are accepted and ignored, and AmbientTransitionListener isn’t called. | . | Paired phone | The phone’s bridged notifications and launcher entries aren’t shown on the watch. Both apps are always running, so delivery that starts a stopped app isn’t exercised. | . | Data Layer fidelity | getCapability leaves out the local node, FILTER_REACHABLE is ignored, and onPeerConnected isn’t delivered. ChannelClient has no flow control. Listeners always run on the main thread. | . | Data Layer APIs | The deprecated GoogleApiClient APIs (Wearable.DataApi, MessageApi, …) aren’t simulated. R8-minified builds rename the clients the simulator matches by name, so use a debug build. | . | Wear SDK | Only RemoteInteractionsManager and Watch Face Push are simulated: Sdk.getWearManager returns null for any other service. | . | Without pairing | With neither --pair nor --data-layer agent, the Wearable clients report API_UNAVAILABLE. | . The full design notes are in SIMULATOR_WEAR_LAUNCHER.md, SIMULATOR_WEAR_WATCHFACE_SCENARIOS.md and SIMULATOR_DATALAYER.md.
